svg.text: Canonical capacity and the least-cost dimension repair
Actual N ⊂ M and core S ⊂ R; applies to both canonical rows A and B.
A. Every finite represented central unit has trace at least 1 — 85.1–85.4
Finite unit trace t → at most floor(t) central atoms; finite capacity part is countably atomic.
Example necessary bound: τ(u) = 1/4 → finite K(u) ≥ 4. Infinite-capacity atoms are allowed.
Capacity guarantees existence of a bounded target; it does not guarantee profile closeness.
B. Exact trim and fill: a central-data diagnostic — 85.5–85.9
Weights (1/4, 1/4, 1/2); old dimension ζ = (3, 1, 2); target h = (2, 2, 2).
Capacity (8, 8, ∞): feasible. Bars: 60 pixels per dimension; heights encode region weights.
‖p − q‖₂² = removed trace + added trace = 1/4 + 1/4 = ‖ζ − h‖₁ = 1/2.
C. Feasible scalar profiles and squared amplification — 85.10–85.15
θ z ≤ Kₐ, t = θ τ(z), ρ = ‖ζ − θ z‖₁/t; the error includes all mass outside z.
Delete a common Mₙ: Knew = n²Kₐ, ζnew = n²ζ; k = floor(n²θ), b = 1/(n²θ) < 1.
Exact minimum repair cost Dₙ = ‖n²ζ − k z‖₁; Dₙ / (k τ(z)) ≤ (ρ + b)/(1 − b).
No assumption that u commutes with the smaller center; compare whole projections.
Middle-panel bars encode dimensions and trace costs; capacities are diagnostic, not a core construction.
Proof locators: Theorem85.2 (capacity), Theorem85.4 (optimal repair), Theorem85.6 (rounding).
Human context: Popa 1994, Theorem4.2.2, printed213–214. The scalar-profile input remains explicit.
